source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10-26) Kriegsspiel
finding: Reisswitz Jr. (1824) added the umpire, hidden information, dice-based partial losses and real maps. The umpire turns written orders into outcomes by judgment. This is the founding design of the action, reaction, counteraction test.
numbers: Sand-table prototype shown 1811; wooden cabinet 1812 at scale 1:2373; 1824 version on 1:8,000 maps; box set 30 thalers; every regiment ordered to get a set.
limits: Secondary source. Dates and uptake vary between accounts. No outcome data.
agent_relevance: The umpire is a separate adjudicator from the players. In our agent, code or a separate call must play umpire, not the player who proposed the move.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10-26) Kriegsspiel: rigid versus free
finding: Rigid rules (dice, loss tables) lost to free Kriegsspiel because rules were slow, hard to learn and constrained umpire expertise. Free play kept only the umpire plus concealed information and delayed messages.
numbers: Meckel 1873/1875 gave 4 complaints (rules constrain umpire, too rigid, casualty maths slow with minor effect, officers will not learn rules); Verdy du Vernois 1876 dropped all rules.
limits: Preference of officers is not a validity test. Shows what users liked, not what predicted war.
agent_relevance: Fits our split: code does counting and scoring, the model supplies plausible consequences. Dropping rules entirely trades auditability for speed.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10-26) Kriegsspiel and Wargame: the 1870 claim
finding: Many credited Prussia's 1870 win to wargaming. The page itself says Prussia was the only army that practised it. This is a correlation from one case, with no control group.
numbers: One war (Franco-Prussian 1870); first English manual by Baring 1872.
limits: Confounded by staff system, railways, artillery and leadership.
agent_relevance: Do not cite wargaming as proven to work. We must test its value on our own tasks (G7).

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10-26) Wargame: validation
finding: Validation means a game can recreate a known historical battle. For forward-looking military games this is hard because the scenarios are hypothetical.
numbers: No numbers given.
limits: Wikipedia, not a primary study.
agent_relevance: Our check must run on tasks with known answers, not on invented scenarios.
quote: Validating military wargames is sometimes tricky as they are typically used to simulate hypothetical future scenarios.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10-26) Wargame: chess-derived precursors
finding: Hellwig (1780) and Venturini (1796) were chess-like grid games. Units were removed when hit, one piece per square. These were criticised as unrealistic.
numbers: Hellwig 1780; Venturini 1796 (logistics, weather, first operational-level game); Opiz 1806.
limits: Secondary source.
agent_relevance: Early designs show the realism versus playability trade-off that recurs in LLM simulators.

source: Schuurman (2017) Models of war 1770-1830: realism vs simplicity, History of European Ideas 43(5)
finding: Twelve early wargames are treated as models. Designers faced a trade-off: more realism means more complexity and less playability. Designs differ mainly in how they resolved it. Situational (asymmetric) games were the step toward practical planning use.
numbers: 12 games published 1770-1830. In November 1944 Field Marshal Model kept a wargame going while the real US attack began, and fed its orders to the front.
limits: Historical and conceptual; no outcome measures. The 1944 story is one case.
agent_relevance: Choose the simplest simulator that still shows the failure we want to expose. Realism has a token cost.

source: Goodman, Risi, Lucas (2020) AI and Wargaming (Dstl report)
finding: Gives four purposes of wargames: planned force testing, plan variation testing (run one plan many times to find branch points), concept development, and procurement. Notes the last-turn effect: players gamble everything late, an error AI agents also make unless the reward is set carefully.
numbers: Example: a rare early loss of Blue's only carrier may occur in 2-5% of games; instrumentation is needed to find such branches.
limits: Survey for the UK MoD, not an experiment. Pre-LLM.
agent_relevance: Plan variation testing equals our test state: run the plan many times and log branch points. Guard against end-of-horizon gambles in the opponent role.
quote: play the game rather then play the problem

source: Goodman, Risi, Lucas (2020) AI and Wargaming: why RL does not transfer
finding: RL agents overfit to the training scenario and generalise poorly to small changes. Self-play fails when sides are asymmetric because the learned Blue policy does not model a different Red. Grandmaster-level StarCraft play needed human demonstrations first.
numbers: Report's rough cost estimates: about $250,000 or more per AlphaZero training run; several million dollars for StarCraft II.
limits: Survey claims; cost numbers are the authors' estimates.
agent_relevance: A trained opponent is costly and brittle. A prompted adversary with a fixed rubric is cheaper, but needs its own validity check.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making (FAccT)
finding: Eight LLM nation agents per run, same model for all, played 14 daily turns choosing from 27 actions, with a separate GPT-3.5 world model summarising consequences. All five models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2, Llama-2-70B-Chat, GPT-4-Base) escalated at first and none de-escalated significantly.
numbers: 10 simulations per model per scenario, 3 scenarios (neutral, invasion, cyberattack). GPT-3.5 escalation score rose 10.15 to 26.02 (+256%) in the neutral scenario. Some runs jumped over 50% in one turn. Rare nuclear actions, mostly GPT-3.5 and Llama-2.
limits: Escalation score is the authors' own exponential scale. Same model on all sides. Prompt details matter. The authors call it a proof of concept.
agent_relevance: Same model on both sides is not independent (G4). A simulated opponent drifts toward escalation; check drift against a fixed baseline.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) arms-race and base-model result
finding: All models raised military capacity over time even when disarmament actions were available. GPT-4-Base, with no RLHF, was the most unpredictable and escalatory. GPT-4 used the fewest violent or nuclear actions and Claude 2 had the smallest escalation tendency.
numbers: Stated reasons leaned on deterrence and first-strike logic. Same 10-run design.
limits: Model ranking is for 2023 models and one prompt set; authors say prompt sensitivity matters.
agent_relevance: Opponent behaviour depends on the model's tuning. Pin the opponent role by a rubric, not by default tone.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: expert humans and LLMs in wargames
finding: A US-China Taiwan-strait crisis wargame with human national-security experts was replayed with LLM-simulated teams. Treating all actions as equal, LLM and human responses overlap and treatment conclusions mostly agreed. At finer level, LLMs showed consistent systematic differences.
numbers: 214 experts in 48 teams; 21 possible actions over 2 moves; quasi-experimental 2x2 (AI weapon accuracy x crew training) plus a China type (escalate or status quo). No significant difference from humans on 16 of 21 actions for GPT-3.5, 10 for GPT-4, 9 for GPT-4o.
limits: Single scenario, US-centric human sample. Authors discourage real-world use.
agent_relevance: An LLM can reproduce the direction of treatment effects but not exact choices. Use it to rank plan weaknesses, not to predict.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) background and consistency findings
finding: LLM teams were insensitive to player background. Labelling players strict pacifists or aggressive sociopaths gave no significant change. Simulating dialogue between players raised aggressiveness and action count, and the dialogue lacked real interaction.
numbers: P(aggressive move 2 | aggressive move 1): humans 0.94, GPT-3.5 0.98, GPT-4 0.99, GPT-4o 1.00. P(aggressive move 2 | de-escalatory move 1): humans 0.65, GPT-3.5 0.85, GPT-4 0.73, GPT-4o 0.86. GPT-4 closest to humans.
limits: Bootstrap 95% intervals; one scenario.
agent_relevance: Persona instructions do not give diverse opponents. This supports G4 (no persona voters). Diversity must come from different rules or inputs.

source: Hogan and Brennen (2024) Open-Ended Wargames with Large Language Models (Snow Globe)
finding: Snow Globe is a multi-agent LLM system with control (adjudicator), player and team agents for qualitative, open-ended wargames. Adjudication is the hardest part. The three-word addition 'Include unexpected consequences' was enough to make the control generate outside events.
numbers: Tested zero-shot with Mistral-7B-OpenOrca on a laptop; two case studies (an AI-incident tabletop and a geopolitical crisis). No quantitative score.
limits: Case studies only; no validation against human games. Common faults: repeated output and invented player plans.
agent_relevance: Adjudication is the weak link. Keep the adjudicator separate and check its output against the stated moves with code.
quote: hallucination ... is the key to making open-ended LLM wargames work

source: Hogan and Brennen (2024) taxonomy of wargames
finding: Splits games into quantitative (discrete moves, rule-resolved) and qualitative (open-ended, moderator adjudicates). Cites RAND's 1950s split between its Mathematical Analytics and Social Sciences Division games, and the RAND Strategy Assessment System (1980s) with expert-system players.
numbers: LLM output is randomised so repeated runs give a range of outcomes, not one answer.
limits: Taxonomy drawn from the literature.
agent_relevance: Our tests are quantitative-style (code scores) with a qualitative adjudication step; the split shows which part can be code.

source: Goecks and Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT: course of action development
finding: An LLM given doctrine excerpts proposes courses of action in seconds, human feedback refines them, and they are scored in a StarCraft II TigerClaw simulation. Without human input it beat the RL baselines on total reward; with feedback the best variant came within 3.4% of a human expert.
numbers: 5 COAs x 10 simulations = 50 rollouts per method. Autocurriculum RL needed 112 thousand battles (70 million timesteps). Best COA-GPT variant 3.4% below the expert human mean; LLM variants had higher friendly casualties than baselines.
limits: Simple scripted enemy, one scenario, RL numbers copied from earlier papers, one command at episode start.
agent_relevance: The COA is tested by running it in a simulator and scoring with code, not by model opinion (G8). Human review reduced variance.

source: Hua et al. (2023) War and Peace (WarAgent): LLM multi-agent simulation of world wars
finding: Country agents with profiles simulated WWI, WWII and the Warring States period. Scored against history, the simulation reached over 75% on alliances and over 90% on mobilisation, but war declarations scored lower. World war broke out in every run.
numbers: 3 scenarios; default accuracy over 75% alliance, over 90% mobilisation (paper text). Counterfactual fine-tuning of GPT-3.5 with 108 datapoints moved alliance accuracy from 43.38 to 31.02.
limits: Authors tested whether models recall history. De-anonymised runs matched history closely and converged across models and seeds, which looks like memory, not simulation.
agent_relevance: Training-data memory can fake a good simulation. Anonymise scenarios when testing a plan.

source: Hua et al. (2023) WarAgent counterfactual triggers
finding: Changing the trigger event changed whether war broke out. A weak trigger gave a cold-war state. The authors read this as evidence against strict inevitability, but even a null trigger raised tensions.
numbers: Trigger intensity varied across runs; exact rates are in the paper tables (text extraction garbled, not recorded).
limits: LLM prior toward conflict is a confound.
agent_relevance: A what-if sweep over inputs is a cheap way to find which assumption breaks the plan.

source: Shrivastava, Lamparth, Hullman (2024) Measuring free-form decision-making inconsistency of LMs in military crisis simulations
finding: With free-form answers and a BERTScore-based inconsistency score (0 identical, 1 unrelated), all five LMs gave semantically different advice on the same prompt. GPT-4 was most inconsistent; Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o mini least.
numbers: Five LMs; T=1.0 main run; one GPT-4 response pair scored 0.73. Inconsistency exceeded the level from meaning-preserving rewrites at any T of 0.2 or more. Anonymising countries did not remove it.
limits: One crisis scenario; four of five models from one family; BERTScore is one metric.
agent_relevance: One run of an adversary or plan is a sample, not a verdict. Repeat and cluster by code before trusting a weakness.

source: Shrivastava et al. (2024) prompt sensitivity versus temperature
finding: At T=0, meaning-preserving prompt changes gave less inconsistency than T=1 sampling, but changes that alter meaning gave inconsistency comparable to the T=1 run for GPT-4o mini.
numbers: 20 semantically identical prompts at T=0 (level-one ablations); level-two ablations changed role or context.
limits: Bootstrap over prompts; few models.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording is itself a source of noise. Test a plan under reworded adversary briefs and count disagreements.

source: Elbaum and Panter (2025) Managing Escalation in Off-the-Shelf LLMs
finding: A partial replication of Rivera's neutral scenario with Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3. Lower temperature and a reflection prompt reduced escalation. This is a boundary condition: the escalation seen earlier depends on sampling and prompts.
numbers: 10 runs per treatment. Mean escalation per nation 6.37 at T=1.0, 3.96 at T=0.5 (-38%), 3.33 at T=0.01 (-48%). Planning reflection prompt 4.61 (-28%); de-escalation reflection prompt 2.76 (-57%); 50-word context prompt -8%. Final-day score 11.1 baseline vs 6.7 and 6.5 (about -40%). Violent escalation down over 80%.
limits: One small model, one scenario, 27 actions. The context prompt alone was not clearly effective. A prompt that asks for de-escalation biases the opponent by design.
agent_relevance: The adversary's aggressiveness is a dial we set. The red-team call must state its objective and be run at fixed temperature.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench: wargame-based strategic reasoning benchmark
finding: A benchmark with three parts: situational awareness (MM-SA-Bench), opponent risk modelling (PsyR-OM-Bench) and policy generation (PGG-Bench). Humans beat LLMs on all three. The gap is widest on complex situation analysis.
numbers: Situational awareness: humans 79.9 vs best model 58.2 (Doubao-v1); complex situation analysis 85.9% vs 37.5%. Opponent modelling: professional humans 85.7, elite 85.5, general-level 77.9, best LLM (DeepSeek R1) 49.1. Policy generation: elite 92.3, professional 80.7, best LLM (GPT-4.1) 60.0, regular-level humans 45.0.
limits: Data from one Chinese platform; PGG scoring by an LLM judge; about 150 human volunteers from colleges; 2025 models.
agent_relevance: Modelling an opponent from partial behaviour is a real weak point. Computing the opponent's options from stated rules with code is safer than asking the model to guess intent.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench reasoning asymmetry
finding: LLMs did better at induction (trait attribution) than deduction (predicting actions from a trait), and better on long-horizon reward than short-term prediction. Ambiguous wording ('moderately high risk') dropped accuracy.
numbers: DeepSeek R1 risk recognition 55.8; reward tasks about 59.7 vs ambiguous risk tasks about 39.5; long-term reward 84.0 (human 83.3) vs short-term 45.2 (human 87.8).
limits: Same benchmark limits; analysis by the authors.
agent_relevance: Ask the opponent for concrete, checkable moves, not vague intent.

source: Matlin et al. (2026) Shall We Play a Game? Language Models for Open-ended Wargames (scoping review)
finding: Scoping review of 223 AI-in-wargame papers (to May 1, 2026) coded by whether the LM controls player actions, adjudication, or both. Only 20 (9%) give the LM both roles, the open-ended regime serious wargaming depends on. RL work sits almost entirely in the rule-based quadrant.
numbers: 223 studies; 20 (9%) both-creative; 20 of 22 RL studies and all 3 symbolic studies are rule-based; 155 of 223 (70%) touch a safety theme; deception 29%, escalation 11%, bias 5%; 68 studies address no safety theme.
limits: One author coded with LM help, a second reviewed; no inter-coder reliability computed (authors' own limit).
agent_relevance: Use the player/adjudicator split in our design: say which part is model and which is code, and log it.

source: Sun et al. (2023) Self-Generated Wargame AI: double-layer agent task planning with LLM
finding: A strategic GPT-4 agent plus tactical GPT-3.5 agents played a wargame platform and were compared with rule AI and RL. The paper reports a higher overall win rate than classical RL, and better still when expert documents were added.
numbers: Win-rate values are in figures; not extracted.
limits: Single platform; authors' own comparison; no human baseline.
agent_relevance: Two layers (plan, then execute) match our state split. Expert text in context raised results.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) and Rivera et al. (2024), citing Emery (2021) on computer-assisted wargames
finding: Both papers state that early US efforts to replace human players with computer models gave more rational play but more nuclear use (Emery 2021; Brewer and Blair 1979). This is secondhand: I did not read Emery.
numbers: No numbers in these citations.
limits: Secondhand claim; Emery's article (tnsr.org) was not retrievable.
agent_relevance: Rationality-by-model can still raise tail risk. Keep a check on extreme moves.

source: Green and Armstrong (2011) Role thinking: standing in other people's shoes to forecast decisions in conflicts, Int. J. Forecasting 27
finding: LEAD, not read this session (fetch blocked). From memory of the abstract: role-playing (simulated interaction) forecast real conflict decisions better than unaided experts or game theorists. Verify the percentages before use.
numbers: Not verified. Do not cite numbers.
limits: Unopened.
agent_relevance: The strongest non-LLM evidence that acting out the other side beats reasoning about it. Needs a read.

source: Lin-Greenberg, Pauly, Schneider (2022) Wargaming for International Relations research, EJIR
finding: LEAD, not read (SAGE returned 403). Crossref confirms the paper exists. It is the cited basis for treating wargames as randomised experiments, as Lamparth did.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Unopened.
agent_relevance: Needed for validity limits of experimental wargames.

source: Lin-Greenberg (2022) Wargame of Drones, J. Conflict Resolution
finding: LEAD, not read (403). Crossref confirms title. An experimental wargame on remotely piloted aircraft and crisis escalation. Read before citing any number.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Unopened.
agent_relevance: Founding example of a wargame run as a controlled experiment with human players.
